ImageDescription.value: The Pavilion Wing of Osborne House from the south-west. Osborne House is a summer home and rural retreat near East Cowes on the Isle of Wight, designed for Queen Victoria by her husband Prince Albert, and built between 1845 and 1851. The house is a grade I listed building in England.

Adam Osborne posing with the Osborne 1 for the Oakland tribune


Osborne awaiting gold and glory from computer

By CLIFF PLETSCHET

He won't push the assembly-line button for another two months, but Adam Osborne sees nothing but gold and glory in the flourishing, fascinating world of computer technology. He talks brazenly about knocking over competition at home and abroad with his "baby," CLIFF Osborne 1, a portable, personal business computer that he touts as lower in weight and price than any other currently on the market. It's pretty bold talk for someone who has not yet started production. But if you follow the 42- year-old Osborne around his still-empty Hayward plant as he points out where "assembly" will go, where "warehousing" will go, where "clerical" will go, his fervor can be infectious. In his mostly-bare office is one desk and upon it rests a prototype of Osborne 1.

Osborne sits on the edge of one and holds court. "We just took an order from Japan," he announces excitedly. "We can turn the tables on Japan. That goes for all of us. Even the auto industry." He freely comparing the attributes of his Osborne 1 with the products of glamorous Apple Computer Inc.

of Cupertino. He contends Osborne 1 will sell for $1,800 after production starts in June - while Apple charges $5,000 for "all-in all comparable equipment." He admits an Apple computer is more expandale and offers a color rather than a blackand-white screen. However, he further claims, computer will have a greater memory capacity than an Apple 64,000 characters to 48,000 characters. He also notes that Osborne 1 will be portable while "it takes at least 10 minutes to take an Apple apart" for moving. Apple has to charge so much more, he contends, because the firm is "over-staffed" at 1,500 employees.

"In 12 months we'll match their volume with 200 people," he brashly predicts. Is Apple worried about Osborne? Frederick M. Hoar, Apple's public relations chief, says he's more confused than concerned. He observes that if Osborne is comparing his computer with Apple II, then he's off on the price because Apple II starts at $2,500. If he's comparing it with Apple III which sells for $4,000 to $5,000 - then he's off on memory because Apple III holds up to 128,000 characters.

Hoar brands as "poppycock" Osborne's conthat Apple has 1,500 employees 1,000 who tention that Apple is overstaffed. He, confirms were hired in the past 12 months - but he notes that sales-per-employee are now running about $200,000, a figure he terms "extremely rare" in an American business. Osborne studied chemical engineering in college and joined Shell Development Co. in Emeryville in 1967. There he was first exposed to computers.

When Shell moved to Texas, Osborne struck out on his own as a computer consultant. He started to publish manuals and then books. Soon he formed a Berkeley publishing company specializing in books about computer technology. Last year, Osborne sold the publishing comto McGraw-Hill Inc. and decided to go into pany computer production.

Is Osborne "invention?" Not exactly, he says. He bought different parts from different firms like the display terminal from giant Motorola Inc., the discs from small MPI of Los Angeles, the keyboard from Datametrics Corp. of Van Nuys - "seeking out the best parts and the best prices." In all, the parts of 12 firms are represented in the prototype. his Osborne, who lives with his wife and two children in Berkeley, is cagey about his firm's financial position. He says it's capitalized at "less than $1 million" by 25 investors, himself included.

He now owns a majority interest, but not for long. Stock options available to his partners but not to: him will cut into his share. "It's too late for anyone to get in, even my neighbors," he says: "We've got all the money we need." Osborne also declines to reveal how many production orders he's received, but admits to a shot-in-arm from a recent mention in the Wall Street Journal. He will not sell to individuals, but is taking 10-percent refundable deposits from individuals "which promises them delivery (from a supplier) in 1981 instead of 1982." won't say how many suppliers he's attracted to date. Osborne - who's showing off Osborne 1 at the West Coast Computer Faire in the Civic Auditorium in San Francisco this weekend doesn't consider himself a computer whiz.

"I designed my machine on the basis of known technology," he says. "I didn't do anything that anyone else couldn't have done.".
